---
title: "What Does a Typical Correlation Look Like?"
description: |
  The effect-size benchmarks people cite for individual-differences research
  come from coded effects in meta-analyses. IRW can come at the question from
  two other directions: whole correlation matrices as authors published them,
  and item-level matrices computed from raw responses across a random sample
  of core tables. This pilot puts the two side by side.
date: today
format:
  html:
    code-fold: true
    toc: true
    toc-depth: 2
execute:
  echo: true
  message: false
  warning: false
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| echo: false

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(tibble)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 13))
irw_blue  <- "#2166ac"
irw_red   <- "#d73027"
irw_amber <- "#b8791f"
irw_grey  <- "grey50"

cache_path   <- "typical_correlation_data/typical_correlation_results.rds"
rel_path     <- "typical_correlation_data/rel_ceiling.rds"
matched_path <- "typical_correlation_data/matched_rses.rds"
cache_ok <- file.exists(cache_path) && file.exists(rel_path) && file.exists(matched_path)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = cache_ok)

f2 <- function(x) sub("^(-?)0\\.", "\\1.", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2))
pct <- function(x) paste0(round(100 * x), "%")
`%||%` <- function(a, b) if (is.null(a)) b else a
```

```{r}
#| label: cache-warning
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| output: asis
if (!cache_ok) {
  cat("::: {.callout-warning}\n## Results cache not found\n\n",
      "Run `vignettes/typical_correlation_compute.R`, `typical_correlation_rel.R` and ",
      "`typical_correlation_matched.R` from the repository root to generate it.\n:::\n", sep = "")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: load
#| echo: false
.c <- readRDS(cache_path)
date_run <- .c$date_run

# ---- published side ----
cov_meta <- .c$cov_meta
pub_all  <- .c$pub_cells |> filter(!is.na(r))
pub      <- pub_all |> filter(!overlap_dropped)
pub$matrix <- paste(pub$table, ifelse(is.na(pub$group), "", pub$group))

n_pub_tables_all <- n_distinct(pub_all$table)
n_pub_tables     <- n_distinct(pub$table)
n_pub_matrices   <- n_distinct(pub$matrix)
n_pub_cells      <- nrow(pub)

pub_table <- pub |>
  group_by(table) |>
  summarise(med_abs = median(abs(r)), med = median(r), share_neg = mean(r < 0),
            n_cells = n(), n_med = median(n, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
pub_matrix <- pub |>
  group_by(table, matrix) |>
  summarise(med_abs = median(abs(r)), n_med = median(n, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

# cell-level quantiles with each table weighted equally (1 / cells in table)
wq <- function(x, w, p) {
  o <- order(x); x <- x[o]; w <- cumsum(w[o]) / sum(w)
  vapply(p, function(pp) x[which(w >= pp)[1]], numeric(1))
}
pub$w_table <- 1 / ave(rep(1, nrow(pub)), pub$table, FUN = sum)
q_pub_tab  <- wq(abs(pub$r), pub$w_table, c(.25, .5, .75))
q_pub_cell <- quantile(abs(pub$r), c(.25, .5, .75))
q_pub_n    <- wq(abs(pub$r), ifelse(is.na(pub$n), 0, pub$n) * pub$w_table * n_distinct(pub$table), c(.25, .5, .75))
q_pub_mat  <- wq(abs(pub$r), 1 / ave(rep(1, nrow(pub)), pub$matrix, FUN = sum), c(.25, .5, .75))
q_pub_sgn  <- wq(pub$r, pub$w_table, c(.25, .5, .75))

# ---- subject tags (published) ----
split_tags <- function(x) lapply(strsplit(ifelse(is.na(x), "", x), "\\s*[|;,]\\s*"), function(v) v[nzchar(v)])
tag_pub <- cov_meta |>
  filter(table %in% pub_table$table) |>
  select(table, construct_type) |>
  mutate(tag = split_tags(construct_type)) |>
  unnest(tag) |>
  distinct(table, tag)

# ---- core side ----
core_cells <- .c$core_cells |> filter(!is.na(r))
core_meta  <- .c$core_meta
core_info  <- .c$core_info
core_fail  <- .c$core_fail
core_meta$gap <- core_meta$mean_abs_item_rest_r - core_meta$mean_item_rest_r
low_gap <- core_meta$table[!is.na(core_meta$gap) & core_meta$gap < 0.005]

core_table <- core_cells |>
  group_by(table) |>
  summarise(med_abs = median(abs(r)), med = median(r), share_neg = mean(r < 0),
            med_abs_pearson = median(abs(r_pearson), na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(core_info, by = "table") |>
  mutate(low_gap = table %in% low_gap)
core_cells$w_table <- 1 / ave(rep(1, nrow(core_cells)), core_cells$table, FUN = sum)
q_core_tab  <- wq(abs(core_cells$r), core_cells$w_table, c(.25, .5, .75))
q_core_pear <- with(core_cells[!is.na(core_cells$r_pearson), ],
                    wq(abs(r_pearson), w_table, c(.25, .5, .75)))
lg <- core_cells[core_cells$table %in% low_gap, ]
q_core_lg_sgn <- wq(lg$r, lg$w_table, c(.25, .5, .75))
q_core_lg_abs <- wq(abs(lg$r), lg$w_table, c(.25, .5, .75))

core_tags <- .c$core_tags
tag_core <- if (!is.null(core_tags)) {
  core_tags |>
    filter(table %in% core_table$table) |>
    select(table, construct_type) |>
    mutate(tag = split_tags(construct_type)) |>
    unnest(tag) |>
    distinct(table, tag)
} else tibble(table = character(), tag = character())

# ---- reliability ceiling ----
rel <- readRDS(rel_path)$cells |> filter(!is.na(r), !is.na(ceiling))
# ---- matched RSES ----
mt <- readRDS(matched_path)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## This is a pilot

The published side uses every matrix in `irw_cov` (`r n_pub_tables_all` tables). The core side uses a seeded random sample of `r .c$n_core_sampled` of the `r format(.c$n_eligible, big.mark = ",")` eligible core tables, each capped at `r format(.c$max_people, big.mark = ",")` randomly chosen people and `r .c$max_items` randomly chosen items. Numbers will move when the core pass is run on everything. The design is under discussion in [datapages/irw#451](https://github.com/datapages/irw/issues/451); comments there are welcome.
:::

## The question

How big is a typical correlation? The benchmarks most often quoted for individual-differences research are Gignac and Szodorai's (2016): from 708 meta-analytically derived correlations, the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles were .11, .19 and .29, which they suggested reading as small, typical and relatively large. Bosco et al. (2015) did the same for applied psychology from 147,328 coded correlations in metaBUS and got a median |r| of .16.

Both are built from correlations that someone coded one at a time. IRW holds two other kinds of evidence:

- **Published matrices** (`irw_cov`). Whole correlation and covariance matrices as authors printed them: mostly correlations *between scales*, chosen for a model the authors wanted to fit.
- **Core response data.** Any core table can be turned into an item-by-item correlation matrix with `irw_fetch(<table>, source = "cov")`. These are correlations *between items within one instrument*, computed the same way for every table, with nobody choosing which cells to print.

The two answer different questions, and the gap between them is the interesting part.

## Published matrices

```{r}
#| label: pub-summary
#| echo: false
n_dropped_tables <- n_pub_tables_all - n_pub_tables
```

After keeping one table from each group of tables that share a sample (this drops `r n_dropped_tables` tables, using the `overlaps` record field), the published side has `r n_pub_tables` tables, `r format(n_pub_matrices, big.mark = ",")` matrices and `r format(n_pub_cells, big.mark = ",")` off-diagonal cells. Covariances were converted to correlations. Each table counts once: a table's cells share its weight, so the large meta-analytic corpora (some tables hold dozens of matrices) don't swamp the result.

With that weighting, the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles of |r| are **`r f2(q_pub_tab[1])`, `r f2(q_pub_tab[2])` and `r f2(q_pub_tab[3])`**. That is well above the Gignac and Szodorai benchmarks (.11, .19, .29).

```{r}
#| label: fig-pub-dist
#| fig-cap: "Median |r| per published table. Dashed lines: Gignac and Szodorai's 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles."
#| fig-height: 4
ggplot(pub_table, aes(med_abs)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.025, boundary = 0, fill = irw_blue, colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(.11, .19, .29), linetype = "dashed", colour = irw_red) +
  labs(x = "median |r| within the table", y = "tables")
```

The weighting choice matters less than one might expect:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-pub-weights
#| echo: false
tibble(
  weighting = c("each table equally (headline)", "each matrix equally", "each cell equally",
                "each table equally, then by sample size", "each table equally, signed r"),
  p25 = c(q_pub_tab[1], q_pub_mat[1], q_pub_cell[1], q_pub_n[1], q_pub_sgn[1]),
  p50 = c(q_pub_tab[2], q_pub_mat[2], q_pub_cell[2], q_pub_n[2], q_pub_sgn[2]),
  p75 = c(q_pub_tab[3], q_pub_mat[3], q_pub_cell[3], q_pub_n[3], q_pub_sgn[3])
) |>
  mutate(across(p25:p75, f2)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Weighting", "25th", "50th", "75th"), align = "lrrr")
```

Signs are kept in the last row. Between-scale signs depend on how each scale was scored, so the signed distribution is only a rough guide, but `r pct(mean(pub$r < 0))` of published cells are negative.

### By subject

The cov subject tags give each matrix a construct type. A table carrying more than one tag counts in each.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pub-tags
#| fig-cap: "Median |r| per published table, by construct-type tag. The number of tables is on the right."
#| fig-height: 4.5
tp <- pub_table |> inner_join(tag_pub, by = "table")
lev <- tp |> group_by(tag) |> summarise(m = median(med_abs), k = n()) |> arrange(m)
tp$tag <- factor(tp$tag, levels = lev$tag)
ggplot(tp, aes(med_abs, tag)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, fill = "grey92") +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.15, alpha = 0.35, size = 1, colour = irw_blue) +
  geom_text(data = lev, aes(x = 1.02, y = tag, label = k), hjust = 0, size = 3.3, colour = irw_grey) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1.08)) +
  labs(x = "median |r| within the table", y = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: pub-tag-numbers
#| echo: false
lev_k <- lev |> filter(k >= 10)
hi <- lev_k |> slice_max(m, n = 1); lo <- lev_k |> slice_min(m, n = 1)
```

Among tags with at least 10 tables, **`r hi$tag`** matrices run hottest (median `r f2(hi$m)`) and **`r lo$tag`** matrices coolest (median `r f2(lo$m)`). The proposal predicted that attitude and behaviour-model matrices (TPB, UTAUT, TAM) would run hotter than personality or attainment ones. The construct-type tags are coarser than that. The `framework` tag is the sharper test, but so far it is set on only a few tables:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-framework
#| echo: false
fw <- cov_meta |>
  filter(table %in% pub_table$table) |>
  distinct(table, framework) |>
  mutate(fw = split_tags(framework)) |>
  unnest(fw, keep_empty = TRUE) |>
  mutate(grp = case_when(
    fw %in% c("TPB", "TAM", "UTAUT", "RAA", "HAPA", "HBM", "SCCT") ~ "behaviour or technology-acceptance model",
    fw == "status_attainment" ~ "status attainment",
    TRUE ~ "no framework tag")) |>
  distinct(table, grp) |>
  left_join(pub_table, by = "table")
fw_sum <- fw |> group_by(grp) |>
  summarise(tables = n(), median = median(med_abs), q25 = quantile(med_abs, .25), q75 = quantile(med_abs, .75), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(median))
fw_sum |> mutate(across(median:q75, f2)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Framework", "Tables", "Median of table medians", "25th", "75th"), align = "lrrrr")
fwb <- fw_sum |> filter(grp == "behaviour or technology-acceptance model")
fwn <- fw_sum |> filter(grp == "no framework tag")
```

The `r fwb$tables` tables fitted to a behaviour or technology-acceptance model (TPB, TAM, UTAUT, RAA, HAPA, HBM, SCCT) have a median |r| of `r f2(fwb$median)`, against `r f2(fwn$median)` for untagged tables. That is in the predicted direction, but `r fwb$tables` tables is too few to lean on.

## Item-level matrices from core

```{r}
#| label: core-summary
#| echo: false
n_core_ok <- nrow(core_table)
meth <- table(core_info$method)
nm <- function(k) if (k %in% names(meth)) meth[[k]] else 0L
```

The core pass computed an item-by-item matrix for `r n_core_ok` of the `r .c$n_core_sampled` sampled tables (`r nrow(core_fail)` failed; see the end of the page). Binary items got tetrachoric correlations (`r nm("tetrachoric")` tables), items with 3 to 8 categories polychoric (`r nm("polychoric") + nm("polychoric (correct = 0)")`), and anything else Pearson (`r nm("pearson")`). Before estimation each item's codes were recoded to consecutive integers, keeping their order. psych counts categories from the range of the codes, so a 0/5/10/15 item otherwise trips its eight-category limit. For `r nm("polychoric (correct = 0)")` sparse tables, psych's continuity correction for empty cells failed, and those were estimated without it (`correct = 0`). Pearson was also computed on the raw codes for every table, as a check.

Response direction is not harmonised across core items, so a reverse-keyed item stored raw correlates negatively with the rest of its scale. That sign carries no substantive meaning, so the headline uses |r|. Weighting each table equally, the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles of inter-item |r| are **`r f2(q_core_tab[1])`, `r f2(q_core_tab[2])` and `r f2(q_core_tab[3])`**. With Pearson throughout they are `r f2(q_core_pear[1])`, `r f2(q_core_pear[2])` and `r f2(q_core_pear[3])`: the estimator alone moves the median by `r f2(q_core_tab[2] - q_core_pear[2])`.

### Keying: |r| and a known-direction subset

The core metadata carries each table's mean item-rest correlation twice, signed (`mean_item_rest_r`) and absolute (`mean_abs_item_rest_r`). If no item correlates negatively with the rest of its scale, the two agree. Tables where they agree to within .005 (`r sum(core_table$low_gap)` of the `r n_core_ok` here) show no sign of reverse keying, so their signed r can be read directly. Only `r pct(mean(lg$r < 0))` of item pairs in this subset are negative, against `r pct(mean(core_cells$r[!core_cells$table %in% low_gap] < 0))` in the rest. This is a proxy, not a keying record: an instrument with negatively correlated subscales can open the gap without any reverse keying.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-keying
#| echo: false
tibble(
  set = c("all sampled tables, |r|", "low-gap subset, |r|", "low-gap subset, signed r"),
  tables = c(n_core_ok, sum(core_table$low_gap), sum(core_table$low_gap)),
  p25 = c(q_core_tab[1], q_core_lg_abs[1], q_core_lg_sgn[1]),
  p50 = c(q_core_tab[2], q_core_lg_abs[2], q_core_lg_sgn[2]),
  p75 = c(q_core_tab[3], q_core_lg_abs[3], q_core_lg_sgn[3])
) |>
  mutate(across(p25:p75, f2)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Set", "Tables", "25th", "50th", "75th"), align = "lrrrr")
```

Restricting to the low-gap subset raises the median from `r f2(q_core_tab[2])` to `r f2(q_core_lg_abs[2])`, and within the subset signed and absolute r agree at these percentiles. But the subset is not a random slice of core. It changes the mix of construct types:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-keying-mix
#| echo: false
tag_core |>
  mutate(low_gap = table %in% low_gap) |>
  count(tag, low_gap) |>
  group_by(low_gap) |> mutate(share = n / sum(n)) |> ungroup() |>
  select(-n) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = low_gap, values_from = share, values_fill = 0) |>
  rename(`flagged` = `FALSE`, `low gap` = `TRUE`) |>
  arrange(desc(`low gap`)) |>
  mutate(across(-tag, pct)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Construct type", "Among tables showing reverse keying", "Among low-gap tables"),
        align = "lrr")
```

```{r}
#| label: keying-mix-numbers
#| echo: false
km <- tag_core |> mutate(low_gap = table %in% low_gap) |> group_by(tag) |>
  summarise(k = n(), flagged = sum(!low_gap), share_flagged = mean(!low_gap), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(k >= 10) |> arrange(desc(share_flagged))
```

Among construct types with at least 10 sampled tables, **`r km$tag[1]`** tables are the most often flagged (`r km$flagged[1]` of `r km$k[1]`), and **`r km$tag[nrow(km)]`** tables the least (`r km$flagged[nrow(km)]` of `r km$k[nrow(km)]`). The worry going in was that the subset would tilt towards binary achievement tests. In this sample it does not: cognitive/educational tables are a small share of both groups. The shift is away from personality scales and towards opinion/attitude scales.

### By subject

```{r}
#| label: fig-core-tags
#| fig-cap: "Median inter-item |r| per core table, by construct-type tag. The number of tables is on the right."
#| fig-height: 4.5
tc <- core_table |> inner_join(tag_core, by = "table")
levc <- tc |> group_by(tag) |> summarise(m = median(med_abs), k = n()) |> arrange(m)
tc$tag <- factor(tc$tag, levels = levc$tag)
ggplot(tc, aes(med_abs, tag)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, fill = "grey92") +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.15, alpha = 0.45, size = 1.2, colour = irw_amber) +
  geom_text(data = levc, aes(x = 1.02, y = tag, label = k), hjust = 0, size = 3.3, colour = irw_grey) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1.08)) +
  labs(x = "median inter-item |r| within the table", y = NULL)
```

## Items versus scales

```{r}
#| label: fig-both
#| fig-cap: "Median |r| per table, published matrices (mostly between scales) and core item-level matrices (within one instrument). Each table counts once."
#| fig-height: 4
both <- bind_rows(
  pub_table |> transmute(side = "published matrices", med_abs),
  core_table |> transmute(side = "core, inter-item", med_abs)
)
ggplot(both, aes(med_abs, colour = side, fill = side)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.2, adjust = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(.11, .19, .29), linetype = "dashed", colour = irw_grey) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(irw_amber, irw_blue)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(irw_amber, irw_blue)) +
  labs(x = "median |r| within the table", y = "density", colour = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Both IRW distributions sit to the right of the coded-effect benchmarks (dashed), and the item-level one sits further right still. Two forces pull in opposite directions. Aggregating items into scale scores raises reliability, which raises observed correlations between scales. But items within one instrument are chosen to measure the same thing, while two scales in a published matrix usually measure different things. In these data the second force wins: within-instrument item pairs correlate more strongly than the between-scale pairs authors print.

### One instrument on both sides: the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale

```{r}
#| label: matched
#| echo: false
pm <- mt$pub
ov_groups <- mt$pub_meta$group[!is.na(mt$pub_meta$overlaps) & mt$pub_meta$overlaps != ""]
pm_ind <- pm[!pm$group %in% ov_groups, ]
m_pub_all <- median(pm$value); m_pub_ind <- median(pm_ind$value)
m_core_poly <- median(abs(mt$core$value)); m_core_pear <- median(abs(mt$core$r_pearson))
share_neg_core <- mean(mt$core$value < 0)
```

The Rosenberg scale is the one instrument confirmed on both sides at the item level. `gnambs_2018_rses10` holds `r n_distinct(pm$group)` published 10-item matrices from Gnambs, Scharl and Schroeders's (2018) meta-analysis. `rosenberg_selfesteem` holds raw responses, of which `r format(mt$n_core_people, big.mark = ",")` randomly chosen respondents were used here.

- **Published:** the median item-pair r across the `r n_distinct(pm$group)` matrices is `r f2(m_pub_all)`. Leaving out the `r length(ov_groups)` matrices whose `overlaps` field says they share data with `rosenberg_selfesteem`, it is `r f2(m_pub_ind)`. The published matrices are recoded so all items point the same way: only `r pct(mean(pm$value < 0))` of cells are negative.
- **Core:** `r pct(share_neg_core)` of item pairs are negative, which is the scale's five reverse-keyed items stored raw. The median |r| is `r f2(m_core_pear)` with Pearson and `r f2(m_core_poly)` with polychoric correlations.

So even with the instrument held fixed, the core sample correlates more strongly than the published samples. The estimator accounts for part of the gap; the rest is sample. Some of Gnambs et al.'s matrices were reconstructed from published loadings, which the table's notes record.

## A reliability ceiling check

```{r}
#| label: rel
#| echo: false
n_rel_tab <- n_distinct(rel$table)
ex <- rel |> filter(exceeds)
ex_tab <- ex |> count(table, sort = TRUE)
```

Two scales with reliabilities $\rho_i$ and $\rho_j$ can correlate at most $\sqrt{\rho_i \rho_j}$, the value reached when their true scores correlate perfectly. `r n_rel_tab` published tables report reliabilities (`rel` rows), covering `r format(nrow(rel), big.mark = ",")` scale pairs. Of these, **`r nrow(ex)` (`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * nrow(ex) / nrow(rel))`) exceed the ceiling**, spread over `r nrow(ex_tab)` tables. The median overshoot is `r f2(median(abs(ex$r) - ex$ceiling))`.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-rel
#| echo: false
ex |>
  group_by(table) |>
  summarise(pairs = n(), max_over = max(abs(r) - ceiling), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(pairs)) |>
  mutate(max_over = f2(max_over)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Table", "Pairs above the ceiling", "Largest overshoot"))
```

A pair above the ceiling is not necessarily an error. Coefficient alpha understates reliability when items are not tau-equivalent, the reliabilities may come from a different sample than the correlations, and latent-variable correlations are not bounded this way. Mostly this flags tables worth a second look at the source.

## Caveats

- **Published matrices are curated.** Authors print the variables they modelled, and IRW's holdings lean on CC BY articles and open deposits. The published side answers "typical in openly licensed published matrices", not "typical in psychology".
- **Core has its own selection:** it holds whatever data people chose to share, and the pilot excludes longitudinal, sparse (density below .5) and very large tables.
- **|r| is biased upward near zero.** Folding noise around zero inflates small correlations. This matters little for inter-item pairs, which mostly sit well above zero, but it is why both sides are summarised with |r| for the comparison.
- **The estimators differ.** Published matrices are mostly Pearson on scale scores, while the core side uses polychoric and tetrachoric correlations, which run higher than Pearson on the same items (see the Pearson figures above).
- **Within- and between-construct pairs are mixed** on the published side. Separating them needs construct labels on variables, which IRW does not have yet.

## What the full run would add

- The core pass on every eligible table, not `r .c$n_core_sampled`, with the subject breakdown by sample and framework tags as well as construct type.
- A fuller `framework` tagging of the published side, so the behaviour-model comparison rests on more than a handful of tables.
- More matched instruments beyond the Rosenberg scale.

```{r}
#| label: failures
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
if (nrow(core_fail)) {
  cat("\n**Core tables that failed in this run:**\n\n")
  cat(paste0("- `", core_fail$table, "`: ", core_fail$error, collapse = "\n"), "\n")
}
```

## Reproducibility

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
```

{{< include ../components/_data-version.qmd >}}

Results were computed on `r format(date_run, "%B %d, %Y")` against `irw_cov` `r .c$irw_version$version[.c$irw_version$dataset == "irw_cov"]`, with the development version of the irw R package, which adds `source = "cov"` (not yet on CRAN). To regenerate:

```r
# from the project root, with the development irw installed
source("vignettes/typical_correlation_compute.R")
source("vignettes/typical_correlation_rel.R")
source("vignettes/typical_correlation_matched.R")
quarto::quarto_render("vignettes/typical_correlation.qmd")
```
